ending_first.ending: At the seventh dawn Cole reaches the chapel with enough blood to pay the ceremony and does not declare it; Lena Cho completes the rite through the memorial-tower door he timed and takes the single purse; Voss cannot stake the credit in Maren's name or his decayed vials; Cole remains in the chapel shade as the window closes and forfeits.
ending_first.cost: Cole loses the purse and the exit; Deacon Ward is already dead, spent to close a guest debt; Maren's credit is real and uncollectable; Voss's correctly run market is worthless; Lena leaves with money and no one left to have been right about.
ending_first.final_image: First light through the chapel door. Lena is gone. Voss's open ledger on a pew shows Maren's line as a credit. Maren holds a cassette that has run out. Cole sits in the doorway shade and steps neither into the rite nor into the sun. The timing notebook lies face-down.

jacket_copy:
Bennington, November 1984. A sealed match. Seven nights. Cole Harlan comes to measure it: hunger clocks, a paper tribute book, hosts who lose the night when they sleep. He wants the single dawn payout at the chapel and no surprises.

Anton Voss is already taxing feeds and selling access to named hosts. Lena Cho reads the people Cole treats as nodes. Julian Marek opens the Whitlock house as a party. In town, a singer named Maren finds bruises and a cassette of a night she does not remember. A campus night-shift man writes everything down.

Guests cannot log out. Stored blood decays. Only the first rite pays. Cole starts a notebook, files a ledger line, and keeps a host off the market as if that were still analysis.

The book will not stay inventory. Neither will she.
plot_summary_short:
The Night Ledger is a science-fiction thriller screenplay set inside a closed virtual match rendered as Bennington, Vermont, in November 1984. Paying players enter as vampire guests for seven nights and cannot log out. They must drink blood from hosts, simulated townspeople who believe they are real, or they weaken and are removed. When a host sleeps, that night is erased from memory, but bruises, tapes, and notes remain. Sunlight destroys a guest. The only paying exit is a chapel ceremony at the seventh dawn: the first guest to complete it with a declared amount of blood-value takes the money and leaves; if no one does, every remaining guest loses.

Cole Harlan, a systems analyst, enters to map these rules and take the payout. Anton Voss already taxes feeding through a paper ledger and sells exclusive rights to named hosts. Maren Ellison, a host and bar singer, finds bruises and a cassette of a night she does not remember and investigates. Cole pays Voss to keep other guests off her; the book records a credit in her name that everyone files as Voss's claim. Lena Cho, a guest who reads people, copies Cole's timing notes as a map to a second chapel door.

At a hillside party, desire breaks Cole's distance from Maren. Voss corners stored blood. Deacon Ward, a host on campus night safety, is killed in a tribute enforcement. Maren stays awake through the last night. At dawn Cole has enough blood-value to finish the ceremony and does not; Voss cannot spend a credit that is not his. Lena completes the rite through the door Cole measured and takes the purse. Cole stays in the chapel shade and forfeits. Maren's credit is never collected.
plot_summary_long:
The Night Ledger is a science-fiction crime thriller written as a screenplay. It takes place inside a closed virtual-reality contest that looks and feels like Bennington, Vermont, in late November 1984, with landlines, cassette tapes, paper books, and no way to reach the outside world. Paying players, called guests, enter for seven nights as vampires under fixed limits: they cannot log out; sunlight destroys a guest's body in the game; they must drink blood from the town's inhabitants or they weaken, frenzy, and are removed with nothing. Those inhabitants, called hosts, are simulated people who believe they are real residents. Telling a host that the town is a game does not wake them and grants no control. When a host sleeps, memory of the hours since the last sleep is erased. Physical marks, recordings, notes, and other people's testimony remain. A host who does not sleep keeps the night. Extracted blood can be poured into stamped glass vials and traded; the stored blood loses strength in about two nights. Fresh blood from the vein is stronger and is not recorded unless someone writes it down. Killing a host removes that person from the town permanently.

The contest has one paying exit. On the seventh dawn a short window opens at a stone chapel by the cemetery. A guest who arrives, states an amount of blood as the price, and completes a fixed ceremony takes a single purse of money and leaves the contest. Only the first successful completion pays. Other guests present are not taken out. If the window closes with no completion, every guest still inside loses. Contracts between guests are not enforced by the contest; hunger, sun, decay, and the single payout are.

Cole Harlan, a systems analyst, enters on the first night to measure these rules and take the purse. He rents a room at a motor court, starts a timing notebook, and feeds as little as the hunger clock allows. Downtown he finds The Hollow, a bar with a stage and a back room lit by old television sets, where a campus band plays and Maren Ellison sings. He also finds the Lodge, a fraternal back office where Anton Voss, a guest who has already begun organizing the town, keeps a paper tribute ledger. Voss taxes other guests for feeding, stamps vials, and sells exclusive access to named hosts. He does this to keep control of a position after a loss he took before this contest, and inside that logic cornering supply is the correct move. Voss prices Cole's first feed and offers terms that would put Cole on the book as a client. Hunger does not let Cole wait for a better offer. Cole pays something and remains a rival.

Maren, who lives in a walk-up over a cassette shop, wakes with bruises her sleep should have removed and finds a cassette from downstairs that holds her own voice from hours she cannot remember. She treats this as a practical problem, not a haunting. Deacon Ward, a host who works night-shift campus safety, writes every incident into a pocket notebook and reads the entries back as fact to people who will not retain them. Lena Cho, a guest and psychologist, watches Cole measure rooms and people; she is better at the second than he is. Julian Marek, a guest with money and appetite, opens the Whitlock house on the hill as a party that is also a place to feed. Cole tests a sleep-erasure on a host where it can be seen, notes an ordinary chapel key, and files a line in Voss's ledger about Maren as Voss's claim on her access.

Cole times Maren's sets at The Hollow and quietly pays more into Voss's book so that other guests cannot buy rights to her. The ledger records this as a credit standing in her name. Cole, Lena, Voss, and anyone who looks treat the line as ownership. Cole tells himself the payment is still analysis: keep a node off the open market. It is the first obligation he will not name. Maren stays awake later, matches the cassette against Deacon's notes and against a song she sings at The Hollow that now means something else, and starts asking questions the town answers with work-talk and shrugs. Voss tightens the tax. Stored vials begin to decay. An enforcer hunts a nonpaying guest through downtown.

Mid-contest Julian holds the Whitlock party. Cocaine, drink, and proximity wreck Cole's working distance from Maren, and what follows is paid for in the morning. Lena asks Cole the question that makes him admit, without using the word, that he has already spent value on a host. Julian flatters and then withholds both compliment and a room. After the party Julian will not come in from a delayed dawn and is destroyed in sunlight, a removal no one bothers to write into the book. Voss uses the chaos to corner remaining vials and named-host rights. Cole's notebook, filled with times and paths, looks to anyone who steals a look like a hunt map.

Lena copies the notebook and files it as a route to a second entrance of the chapel through the memorial tower. She spends that reading to put herself a night ahead of Cole. She is better at people than he is at systems, and he cannot recover the night she took. Cole then learns that he has filed the evidence wrongly. The ledger line on Maren is not Voss's claim. It is Cole's own credit in her name. The notebook is not a hunt map. It is a clock on the window in which Maren can keep a night if she refuses sleep.

Voss sends enforcement to close a guest debt that Cole's delay and the tribute market both created. The cost does not land on either guest. Deacon, who is present because he writes things down and goes to the address, is killed. Maren takes Deacon's pocket book, keeps herself awake through the seventh night, and carries the cassette, the notes, and the bruises toward the chapel because a physical copy is the only testimony the town cannot erase.

At first light three guests reach the chapel by different doors. Cole arrives at the main door with enough undeclared blood to pay the price of the ceremony. Voss arrives with the cornered ledger and vials that have decayed past use; the decisive line in the book is the credit in Maren's name and is not his to declare as a stake. Lena enters through the memorial-tower door Cole timed. Voss cannot declare a stake he does not own. Lena declares hers and completes the ceremony. Cole stands in the doorway with Maren and does not declare. Lena leaves with the purse; the contest ends for her alone. Cole stays in the shade of the chapel as the window closes and loses. Voss is still inside when the window closes and loses. Maren has kept the night. Her credit will never be collected. Deacon is already dead. The ledger balances, and it balances unfairly.
